newsitem.title: THAILAND: Top Khmer Rouge fugitives said hiding in Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Top Khmer Rouge fugitives said hiding in Thailand.

text.p: High-ranking members of the Khmer Rouge loyal to hardliner Pol Pot are hiding in Thailand near the border with Cambodia under the protection of an influential Thai politician, intelligence and rebel sources said on Monday.

Pol Pot's right hand man Noun Chea, Khmer Rouge Defence Minister Son Sen and three aides are among those believed to be in hiding at a warehouse in Klonghaad district about seven km (4.4 miles) from the Cambodian border, they told Reuters.
The hardline fugitives fled to Thailand after dissident Khmer Rouge guerrillas loyal to Ieng Sary ousted them last Monday from their Samlaut base in northwestern Cambodia.
"We arrested two of their soldiers on Saturday and learned that their bosses are hiding in a warehouse in Klonghaad district," one of the dissident Khmer Rouge officials told Reuters by telephone.

A Thai businessman based at the border said he learned that a logging company had brought five Khmer Rouge leaders into the country after October 1. The firm had given them sanctuary in Danchumpol village in Trad province, which is on the border, but they might have moved since then, he said.
A Thai intelligence source also said that the five Khmer Rouge leaders were brought into the country by their Thai business associates but was unable to say exactly where they were located.
"They were brought in by a politician who is influential on the border," the intelligence source said, without giving the name of the Thai politician.
Thai military officials when contacted said they had not heard anything about the presence of the fugitives in Thai territory.

News of the Khmer Rouge presence in Thailand emerged last week after Cambodian co-prime ministers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen wrote to Thai premier Banharn Silpa-archa, asking him for assistance in capturing and returning them.
On Saturday, Ranariddh said Thailand had arrested one of the fugitives but might not extradite him to Cambodia. Thailand yet to comment on his statement.
Bangkok has no extradition treaty with Phnom Penh. It has also refused to send back Cambodian Sing Son who escaped to Thailand after allegedly taking part in an aborted coup in 1994.

Ieng Sary, the foreign minister of the Khmer Rouge regime during its 1975-78 reign of terror in Phnom Penh, broke away from Pol Pot in August, taking with him several thousand followers from former hardline strongholds in northwestern Phnom Malai and Pailin provinces.
The breakaway group has since been fighting its former comrades in a bid to take over the remaining jungle strongholds held by the Maoist faction.
The Khmer Rouge refused to recognise the result of a May, 1993, election in Cambodia despite signing the U.N.-sponsored peace pact that led to the polls.
